item.title: The narrative battle over France’s unrest
item.description:
play video
play video
Video Duration play-arrow
Student protests, police violence and French media obsessed with 'barbarians'.Read more
What began as protests over education has rapidly taken over the streets of France and turned into one of the country’s biggest waves of unrest in years.
Many mainstream media outlets have focused their coverage on the violence and looting rather than on the demands of the demonstrators. A lot of airtime has fixated on who the protesters are and what they look like, often using racist terms. That narrative has been picked up by right-wing movements abroad.
Contributors:
Cole Stangler – author, Paris Is Not Dead, and lecturer, American College of the Mediterranean
Diane de Vignemont – Paris-based journalist
Harrison Stetler – lecturer and writer
Philippe Marliere – professor of French and European politics, University College London
On our radar
Israel’s elections are just days away and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has reverted to a familiar alarmist tactic to consolidate support: hyping an “imminent” threat from Iran and telling the United States that it should “finish the job”. Meenakshi Ravi looks at the messaging.
Olga Rudenko: Independent journalism is the ‘ultimate patriotic act’
More than four and a half years into Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine remains under attack, and its journalists are forced to balance many responsibilities at once.
They are documenting a war that has become more dangerous than ever, countering Russian propaganda efforts and trying to hold their own government to account at a time when the news media have been expected to fall into line. The Kyiv Independent, an online newspaper, has been doing all three since 2021.
The Listening Post spoke with its editor-in-chief and cofounder Olga Rudenko about the pressures of reporting when your country is at war.

Casting her ballot at a polling station in Belgrade on Sunday [Marko Djurica/Reuters]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 25 Oct 202625 Oct 2026
Polls have closed in Serbia’s snap parliamentary election, which saw the highest voter turnout in decades, with a student-backed movement seeking to unseat longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic.
Voting ended at 8pm local time (19:00 GMT) on Sunday, with first indications of the result expected a few hours later.
Recommended Stories list of 2 itemslist 1 of 2Serbia votes in election pitting longtime leader against student movementlist 2 of 2Serbia votes as student-led bloc challenges longtime leader Vucicend of list
The vote will determine whether Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which has governed since 2012, can retain power against a movement born from nationwide anticorruption protests.
The State Election Commission said that voter turnout had reached 64.9 percent by 17:00GMT, ⁠⁠the ⁠⁠highest since ⁠⁠the breakup ‌‌of Yugoslavia in ‌‌1992.
The higher turnout does not show which side gained support.
University of Belgrade researcher Jelena Vasiljevic told Al Jazeera in an interview published on Friday that the SNS had a reliable voter base, while the students needed to attract people who normally did not vote.
Sunday’s voting was also marked by reports of intimidation and procedural problems.
The Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA), an independent election watchdog, said its observers recorded pressure on voters or election workers at almost a third of the 500 polling stations it monitored.
It also reported failures to protect ballot secrecy.

The Ballon d’Or, football’s most prestigious individual honour, will be awarded on Monday, with Harry Kane, Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe among the frontrunners in the men’s category and Spain’s Alexia Putellas the favourite to pick the women’s award for the third time.
Given to the best player of the 2025-26 season, the upcoming ceremony will mark the award’s 70th edition, and the first time it is held outside France.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Yamal, Mbappe in El Clasico spotlight as 40 cameras dedicated to coveragelist 2 of 3What are the top five El Clasico clashes between Barcelona and Real Madrid?list 3 of 3‘A match like no other’: El Clasico awaits a Yamal vs Mbappe showdownend of list
Ahead of Monday’s official gala, here’s everything to know about the award, its history and more:
What is the Ballon d’Or?
The Ballon d’Or is the highest individual award given to a footballer, based on his or her performance in the previous season.
The award was created in 1956 by two sports writers, Gabriel Hanot and Jacques Ferran, from France Football, a French magazine.
Originally, the men’s award was limited to European players, but in 1995 it was expanded to include all players of any origin active at European clubs. Finally, in 2007, it became a global award with all professional footballers being eligible.
The women’s Ballon d’Or started in 2018 when Ada Hegerberg was named the inaugural winner.

Manchester United's manager Michael Carrick after losing to Bournemouth at Old Trafford [Darren Staples/AFP]By AFPPublished On 25 Oct 202625 Oct 2026
Amid increasing pressure on his team and a growing threat to his own position as manager, Michael Carrick says he will do what is best for Manchester United after a 3-0 demolition by Bournemouth plunged his future into doubt.
Winless in eight games in all competitions, the 20-time English champions slipped to within one point of the relegation zone after a damaging defeat at Old Trafford on Sunday.
“It’s a tough situation,” Carrick told British broadcaster Sky Sports. “What is next? I don’t know.
“I’ll always do what’s best for this football club. I’ve said it all along; I don’t change that now. I love what I do. I love the responsibility, but we’ll have to wait and see.”
Asked in a post-match news conference if he expects to be sacked in the coming days, Carrick replied: “I totally understand the situation. I’m not expecting anything in particular, to be honest. I’m carrying on as normal. I love this place.”
Despite a dismal run of results, the United fans largely supported the former midfielder as he made his way off the field at full-time before they turned on the club’s players.
“I have mixed emotions to have that connection with the supporters in the moment we’re in. I need time to digest that,” added Carrick.
“I appreciate their support but the situation is where it’s at. We haven’t been good enough.”Manchester United’s captain Bruno Fernandes did not feature in the match against Bournemouth [File: Darren Staples/AFP]

Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi arrives for a media briefing on the Ebola outbreak in Kampala, Uganda on October 25, 2026 [Abubaker Lubowa/Reuters]By AFP and ReutersPublished On 25 Oct 202625 Oct 2026
Uganda has ordered citizens returning after travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to quarantine for 21 days, as it steps up precautions against the Ebola virus.
Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi announced the measure on Sunday at a news conference in Kampala, as Ebola cases in Kenya and Nigeria raised fresh questions about travellers passing through Uganda.
Recommended Stories list of 2 itemslist 1 of 2Kenya announces second Ebola death, says ‘no evidence’ of community spreadlist 2 of 2WHO warns ‘more complex’ Ebola outbreak now present in 3 African countriesend of list
The country says it has no active infections after ending its own outbreak in July. Returning Ugandans with a history of travel to DRC will have to pay for their quarantine, the Ministry of Health said.
Officials have also strengthened checks at Entebbe International Airport and land crossings, and require all incoming travellers to complete forms recording how they can be contacted.
Uganda declared its Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak over on July 28. It had recorded 20 infections and two deaths, according to the Health Ministry.
Yet Swiss authorities have said a Ugandan-born woman married to a Swiss diplomat contracted Ebola during a visit to Uganda in September.
Nigeria confirmed her infection on October 20, after she had travelled to Abuja, its capital.

The head of Jordan’s Football Association (JFA), Prince Ali bin Hussein, has accused FIFA President Gianni Infantino of hijacking the Asian Football Confederation Congress for political purposes ahead of his re-election bid for a fourth term.
At the AFC’s extraordinary congress in Tokyo on Friday, its president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al-Khalifa endorsed Infantino’s bid for re-election as FIFA president.
